about: The words of the chain relic_theft (Data/encounters/chain_relic_theft_793.json; Design/content/chains/relic_theft.md): the bones of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter in a Frisian boat, 828. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the two news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Einhard, Hilduin, Ratleic, Erembert the steward and Germar the blind man are real; Otbert the deacon, Gozhelm of Saint-Medard and Lupicinus the seller of bones are ordinary invented people. Nothing is quoted: Einhard's account, his letters, the law of 789 and the annals are given in our own plain words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The box from the Main

A young deacon has come down the river from the Main with a box sewn in waxed linen, about as long as a man's arm. He does not put it down to talk. He is asking along the shore for a Frisian who knows the Scheldt.

They say a Frisian will carry anything anywhere if you name the tide. I need Ganda, on the Scheldt, where the Lys comes in. Fifteen days by boat from our house, my lord reckons it. My lord has never rowed it.
I came down the Main this morning on a grain boat. Her master crossed himself when I stepped off. I do not think it was for my sake.
The wine boat that brought me from the Main goes no further. Her master says the sea is for Frisians and fools, and he was not sure which I should look for first.
One box. It does not eat, it does not spoil, and it does not go under the ballast. It lies where I lie.

My lord is abbot at Ganda and is never there. He is at the palace. He writes. The steward at Ganda has a letter by now saying a boat is coming, so somebody will be looking out for you, which I am told is rare for a Frisian.
Name a freight: thirty pennies now and ninety at Ganda
Ask what is in the box before you name anything
Carry him and his box for nothing, for your dead
He counts thirty pennies out of a purse that has more in it than a deacon's should. The box goes under the stern board on a folded sail. He sits down on the board, and that is where he stays.

He says his teacher answers every question with another, and gives you one about a thing that opens and shuts a house. Then he tells you plainly. Two martyrs of Rome, Marcellinus the priest and Peter who drove out devils, or as much of them as his lord can spare for Ganda. The freight is thirty now and ninety there.

He looks at you for some time. Then he says he will write your father's name and your mother's on the list for the altar at Mulinheim, and asks how they are spelt. You do not know. He says the saints will.
The man from Soissons

A priest in a good cloak has been waiting where the boats lie. He knows what you carry and from whom. He waits until the deacon has gone up the bank to find bread, and then he comes down the plank as if it were his own.
A box in waxed linen, a deacon who sleeps on it, a Frisian boat bound for the Scheldt. You people think a river keeps secrets. A river is a road with ears on both banks.

Gozhelm, of Saint-Medard at Soissons. The holy Sebastian came to us from Rome two years ago, by the pope's own gift, and the sick have not left our door since. A house with one great saint soon finds it needs another.

A priest of ours went to Rome with the notary and came home with a share of Marcellinus. After Easter our abbot was made to hand it back at the palace, in front of everyone, to the little man who is abbot of Ganda. My house has not forgotten how that felt.

A boat can lose her way in the mouths of the Scheldt. Nobody blames a boat. Bring the box up the Seine to the landing of Saint-Denis, and the cellarer will count you two thousand pennies and will not ask what road you came. Here is a hundred and twenty, so that you think about it.

And do not say theft to me. If the martyrs did not wish to go, no man could lift them. That is known. The notary lifted them out of their own tomb by night, and they came. Ask yourself what that tells you about them.
They tell me you asked no freight. Then you are a pious man, and a pious man should want the martyrs where the most people will come to them. Ganda is a marsh with sheep on it.
Send him off, and tell the deacon when he comes back with the bread
Take the hundred and twenty, and say you will think about it
Hear him to the end, take nothing, and say nothing to anyone
He takes it calmly and puts his purse away. The deacon, when he hears, takes it less calmly, and eats his bread sitting on the box. That night he sleeps with one arm through the cord.

A hundred and twenty pennies, good ones, new from the palace mint. He does not ask for your word and you do not give it. When the deacon comes back with the bread the priest is looking at another boat, and you are coiling a rope.

He talks well. Before he goes he tells you, for nothing, that the abbot's cellarer is paying a fifth over for Rhine wine against the fair of Saint-Denis. It is the kind of thing a man says to be remembered kindly. It is also true.
What the box does

The men know what lies under the stern board. Nobody told them. The boy has a fever from the river and lies under the fore thwart with his teeth knocking, and the others have been talking low since noon.

The grain boat's men told it at the Main mouth. Where that box lay first, up in the hills, it sweated blood for days, and men dreamed the saints wished to be somewhere else. So they were moved. I would like to know where they wish to be now, before we are over the bar.
The boy asks only to lay his hand on the linen. He says he will keep his eyes shut while he does it.

They are not cargo, and they are not a charm for boatmen. But I say the office beside them at dusk, and a man who stands near while I say it does no wrong. I cannot stop a sick boy from standing near.
And somebody at the last landing gave you silver for nothing. I have steered long enough to know what nothing costs.
You sent that priest up the plank faster than he came down it. The men saw. It is why they are asking you and not just doing it.
Let the deacon say his office at the stern, and the men stand near
The box is freight. Nobody goes near it but the deacon
Wait until the deacon sleeps, and lift the linen yourself

The deacon sings thinly and the men do not know the words. The boy lays two fingers on the linen and takes them away as if it were hot. By the middle of the night he is asleep and wet through, and in the morning he asks for bread.

The deacon sings thinly and the men do not know the words. The boy lays two fingers on the linen. The fever takes its own time after that, as fevers do, but the men pull better for having stood there.
The men say nothing, which is how you know what they think. The deacon thanks you. The boy sweats it out by himself under the fore thwart.

Inside the linen is a box of plain oak, and in the box two bundles in red silk, each no bigger than a loaf. A strip of parchment is tied to each. You can make out an M on one and a P on the other, and after that a clerk's small hand. You sew the linen shut with sail twine. It is neat work, for a sailor.
The seller of bones

A man with a mule's pack and a southern way of talking is selling from a cloth on the landing: a tooth, a knot of hair, a splinter of bone. Each has a name on a strip of parchment. He looks up before you have said who you are.
Felicitas, a rib. Dust from the grave of Agnes, cheap, because dust goes a long way. A pope's finger, the name is a little rubbed. All from Rome. I was there when they were lifted. I held the lamp.
You are the boat with the box. Do not look surprised. Since the notary came over the mountains with his two martyrs, every man on this river who owns a spade is a deacon of Rome.

For a boatman I have something useful. Two bundles in red silk, the labels blank, the weight of two small men. Twelve pennies. I do not ask what a box ought to weigh. I only know that boxes get weighed.
Yes, yes. The old emperor's law. No false names of martyrs, no wanderers deceiving the people. I have heard it read out in six towns. In all six I was selling by the church door while they read it.
A priest in a good cloak asked me this morning what a Frisian boat costs. I said it depends who has already paid for it. He did not laugh. You might.
Buy the two blank bundles (12 d)
Buy the rib with a name on it for your own chest (60 d)
Tell him the deacon has a bishop's ear, and watch him pack
Two bundles in red silk go into your sea chest under the spare line. They weigh what he said. Whose they were he does not say, and it is likely he never knew. A graveyard is a graveyard.

Sixty pennies for a rib the length of your hand and a strip of parchment that says FELICITATIS. He swears to it by three saints, all of whom he has for sale. It may be hers. A bishop could say, if a bishop were asked.

He has the cloth rolled and the mule loaded before you have finished the word bishop. Over his shoulder he says the canons at Ganda are paying anything for wax, since candles go with saints, and that he at least sells what he says he sells: bones.
The blind man of the coast

A blind man is led down to the boats by a child. He has heard that saints are going up the river, and he stops at every stern and asks whether this is the boat. The boatmen say no and look away, though he cannot see them do it.
Germar is my name. I am from the coast here. Six winters I have been blind. They say holy men are going up to Ganda in a boat. Is this the boat? Nobody will tell me, and I cannot look.
I have one penny, and I can bail. I bail well. A blind man is never surprised by water.

My lord wants the name of everyone who comes to them, and where they are from, and what ailed them, and the day. He means to write it all down. Take this one, and I have the first name on the list before we are even there.
You sent the priest of Soissons away without being asked. I think you can be trusted with a blind man.
Take him aboard for nothing
Take his penny and set him to bail
Tell him it is some other boat
The child hands him over the side like a parcel and runs. He finds the bailer by feel and sits with it in his lap, facing the stern. He does not ask where the box is. He seems to know.
You take the penny. It is an old light one, worn nearly smooth. He bails as he said he would, without being told when, and the men stop minding him by the second tide.
He thanks you and goes on down the line of boats, asking. The deacon watches him go and says nothing, and writes nothing.
The ebb

The deacon has gone up to the church to hear the office and will be an hour. It is the first time he has left the box. It lies under the stern board. The ebb has begun to run, and the priest of Soissons stands on the strand with a horse and a servant, a little way off, like a man admiring the view.
An hour. The tide is with you and the wind is fair for the west. By the time he has said his Amen you are a sail. Up the Seine to the landing of Saint-Denis, and ask for the cellarer.
You took my hundred and twenty on the river. I did not give it for your thinking.
You took nothing from me on the river, and I respected that. Now I am offering two thousand, and respect is finished.
Three hours of ebb yet. I say only what the water is doing. What we do is yours to say.
In your sea chest, under the spare line, lie two bundles in red silk with their labels blank.
The blind man sits in the bows with the bailer in his lap. He has turned his face toward the strand, where the voices are.
Wait for the deacon. There will be another ebb
Cast off on the ebb with the box aboard
Tell him to come to the boat after dark, alone
Go up to the church and tell the deacon who is on the strand

You sit on the stern board yourself, for once, and watch the ebb go to waste. The priest waits a while, then mounts. The deacon comes down the path wiping his mouth and finds everything as he left it, and does not know there was anything to find.

If there is anyone aboard who is not yours, he is handed onto the sand first. Then the line comes in and she takes the ebb. Nobody speaks. From the water you can see the church door, and it stays shut a long time. When it opens you are too far off to tell one man from another.
He looks at you, and then at your sea chest, though he cannot know what is in it. He says he will come when the fort has shut its gate, and that he will bring what a horse can carry.

The deacon finishes the psalm first. Then he goes to the count's man at the gate. The priest of Soissons shows a letter with the archchaplain's seal on it, and nobody there dares hold him. He rides. But his name is written down, and yours is written beside it, on the other side of the page.
Two boxes

After dark. The deacon sleeps inside the gate. Under the sail on the bottom boards lie four bundles in red silk, two with names on their labels and two without. The priest of Soissons has brought a lamp he does not light, and a bag that he sets down carefully.

I will not count them and I will not look. What I do not see I need not confess. Put two in my hands and I will put the bag in yours. Nine hundred. The rest was for the Seine, and you are saving me the Seine.
Labels are for clerks. Our cellarer writes a fair hand, and he knows the names.
You have seen the true labels by daylight: an M, a P, and a clerk's small hand. Even in the dark your fingers know which pair has writing on it.
You have never seen inside the linen until now. Two of the four have a strip of parchment with writing on it. That is all there is to tell them apart.
Give him the two you bought. A blank label is his cellarer's business
Give him the martyrs, and tie their labels to the two you bought
Give him nothing. Sew the linen shut and send him up the strand

He takes the two bundles against his chest like a man carrying a child out of a fire, and hands you the bag without letting go of them. The martyrs go back into their oak box. You sew the linen with sail twine by feel. Somewhere west of here a great abbey is about to receive two strangers with honour.

The knots on the labels are a clerk's knots and take longer than they should. Then it is done. He goes up the strand with the martyrs against his chest. In the oak box, under the abbot of Ganda's seal, two strangers lie with borrowed names. The men were told to sleep. You do not think they did.

He stands a while with his bag. Then he says that a man who will not sell is only a man who has not heard the right price, and that he has no more prices. He does not ask for his earnest back. It is not a debt a man can take to court.
Weather in the mouths
The wind backs and hardens, and the sea goes the colour of lead over the banks. There is white water where you have never seen any. The men look at the stern board more than at the sky.
This is only weather. I have had worse with a cargo of cheese, and nobody said the cheese was angry.
At the Main mouth they said the saints sweat blood when they are where they do not wish to be. I am not saying this is that. I am saying the men are saying it.
Skipper, if we vowed them a candle. A big one, the weight of the boy. They could not take that badly.
Or if we put about. There is still a Scheldt behind us.
I slept that night at the landing, as I was told. I sleep lightly. I will say no more about it than that.
Shorten sail, keep the lead going, and lose a day
Stand on under full sail
Vow the martyrs a candle of the boy's weight, and lay by 24 d for the wax
Put about for the Scheldt and take the box where it was sent

A reef in the sail, a man in the bows with the lead, and the banks felt out one by one like stairs in the dark. It costs a day. By evening the wind has gone round and the men have stopped looking aft.

She goes through it with her lee rail under and comes out the far side into flat water and a clearing sky. The steersman says nothing. He has the look of a man who would like it known that he said nothing.
A sea comes aboard over the quarter and takes a man off his feet against the thwart. Ribs, most likely. The box does not shift. Nobody finds that a comfort.

You say it aloud at the stern with your hand flat on the board, and count twenty-four pennies into a rag where the men can see. The wind does not drop. The men do not need it to. They needed something to have been said.

She comes round heavily and takes the wind on the other side. Nobody cheers. One of the men begins to sing, badly, something the deacon sang. Whatever the priest of Soissons gave you he will not see again, and neither will he see the box.
A letter on the coast

The toll man has a clerk beside him today, and the clerk has a letter. A deacon on the Scheldt has written to every bishop between the Rhine and the Seine about a Frisian boat and a box in waxed linen.
I take the king's tenth on what is sold. Nobody sells saints, or nobody says so, and I have no tenth in this. But the bishop's clerk has a letter. He reads. I do not.
A boat of the Frisian build, four men. A box so long, sewn in waxed linen, under the seal of the abbot of Ganda. Carried off on the ebb while a deacon sang the office. Lift your stern board, shipman.
Unless you are bound for some landing I should know of. Boats have passed here on a great man's name before now. I am told to look. I am not always told to find.
I know this boat. She has paid her tenth here like a Christian. That is all I will say for her, and I say it only because it is true.
Say whose landing you are bound for, and let the archchaplain's name do the rest
Forty pennies for the clerk's poor, before the board is lifted
Lift the board. Say the deacon missed his tide, and that you will carry the box back yourself

You say the landing of Saint-Denis, and whose cellarer waits there. The clerk folds the letter along its old folds. He says the boat he was told of had a red sail, he is almost sure. Yours is brown. Anyone can see that.

The clerk says any Frisian can say a great man's name. It takes a hundred pennies and an hour before he agrees that the name may be the right one. He writes down your boat all the same, the strakes and the patch in the sail, and puts it in with the letter.

The clerk's poor are many, he says, and thanks you on their behalf. The letter goes back into his sleeve. The toll man looks at the river through all of it, as a man looks who means to have seen nothing.

You lift the board yourself. The clerk looks at the seal and does not touch it. He says the deacon's letter asks only that the box come to Ganda, and does not say in whose boat, and that he sees no reason to write more than he was asked. It is a long way back, and you have time to think on it.
The bank at Ganda

Where the Lys runs into the Scheldt the canons of Saint Bavo stand on the bank with candles lit in daylight. Boys run along the water ahead of you, shouting. Somebody has been watching this river for days.
Erembert, the abbot's steward. We have had the letter a week, and the boys have been on the bank since. You are the first boat they have not been wrong about.
I came by land, on a borrowed mule, with a letter written out for every bishop on the coast. I see I need not send the rest of them. I will say what happened, and I will say that he came back.
This is the shipman I wrote of. He was offered two thousand on the strand, and he came up to the church to tell me in the middle of a psalm.
And he asked no freight. Write that down too. No, write it somewhere the abbot will read it.

The blind man Germar, from the coast by the Scheldt mouth, was led into the church behind the box. Before the office was sung through he said he could see the candles, and after a while the men who held them.
The blind man Germar was led into the church behind the box and stood through the office with his face turned to the candles. Afterwards a canon led him out again, by the sleeve.

The freight I can pay from the chest. More than that is the abbot's to give, and the abbot is at the palace. Come again when two moons have gone. A letter to the palace and back takes that long, when he answers at all.
Carry the box up to the church with your own men
Hand it over at the bank and see to your boat
Lead the blind man up yourself, behind the box

Four Frisians carry it up from the water on two oars, as you would carry a hurt man, and the canons sing in front and do not know what to do with their hands. The steward counts ninety pennies into yours at the church door. Your men talk about it for a year.

The canons take it from you at the water's edge, and it is gone up the bank among the candles before your line is fast. The steward counts out ninety pennies. The boat needs bailing. A boat always does.

He holds your sleeve the whole way up, and lets go of it at the church door without being told he is there. The steward pays the ninety pennies and asks the blind man's name and yours, and has both written down, though only one will be kept.
The abbot's answer
The abbot's answer has come from the palace. The steward reads it to you standing, because it is short. Behind him a canon is writing names on a sheet: who came, from where, and what left them.
He writes: pay the Frisian well, in good silver and all of it, and ask him what he would have besides. He says the part about the silver twice. He always says the part about silver twice.

A girl from Furnes who was blind. A man from Alphen who left two crutches at the door. Two of our own people from the abbey's land. I have the days for all of them. It goes to the abbot when the feast of Saint Bavo is past, and he will put it in a book.

The deacon told the abbot all of it, the ebb and the turning back. The abbot writes that a greater man's priest did worse and was forgiven in front of the whole palace. But he does not offer you land.

And for the matter on the strand he has spoken to the emperor's people. There is a writing being made this year for merchants who serve the palace: its bearer goes free of toll, save at Quentovic, at Dorestad and at the mountain passes. Your name can stand in one.
The deacon says the linen was sewn with sail twine when it came. I told him boats are wet places and things get mended in them. I would as soon not hear whether I was right.

This year the bones of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, which Ratleic the notary had brought out of Rome, came by boat to the house of Saint Bavo at Ganda, where the Lys meets the Scheldt. Many sick were healed there until the eve of Saint Bavo's feast.
Ask for a plot on the bank by the lay village
Ask for a cloth that has lain on the martyrs
Ask for your name in the emperor's writing, and the plot besides

Seven hundred pennies, and a strip of the bank between the abbey and the village, paced out by the steward himself with a boy carrying the pegs. A yearly rent in wax, which he asks you to begin on at once: six loads, at half again over the price, because the candles do not stop.

Six hundred pennies, and a square of white linen that lay a night and a day on the martyrs' bundles. The canon folds it into a little bag of red silk and ties it with a clerk's knot. It weighs nothing. Your men will not let it be stowed anywhere but the stern.

Fourteen hundred pennies, the strip of bank, and a promise that is kept before winter: a sheet with the emperor's name at the foot and yours in the middle, spelt as a Frank would spell it. The steward says a toll man who cannot read will still know the seal. He adds that the archchaplain's people also know your name now, and will for as long as he is archchaplain.
The abbey does not ask
At the landing of Saint-Denis the cellarer has a cart waiting with a white cloth in it. He does not ask what road you came. He asks only whether the seals are whole.
Whole. Good. The abbot of Ganda's own seal. He will know it again when he is told where it lies. That is a matter between great men, and you and I are small ones, God be thanked.
It will be written that the martyrs turned a Frisian's helm with their own hands, wishing to rest beside the holy Sebastian. I have the first lines already. You are in it, as a wind.
Two thousand, as was said. Or less, and a place on the abbot's ground at the fair. The abbot holds the fair's tolls. A man of ours pays them, in a manner of speaking, to himself.
The clerk on the coast wrote down your boat. Let him. A letter against a man of the archchaplain's goes into a chest and stays there.
You see I was right to give you the hundred and twenty. A man thinks better with silver in his hand. I have always found it so.

This year the bones of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, sent by boat to Ganda, came instead to the house of Saint Medard at Soissons. The abbot of Ganda complained of it at the palace and was not heard.
Take the two thousand, and the abbey's name over yours
Take thirteen hundred and a plot on the abbot's ground at the fair
Take six hundred for the freight, and ask that the monks name you in their prayers

Two thousand pennies, counted in tens on the tail of the cart, beside the box, with the white cloth turned back so that it should not be touched by money. The cellarer says you may call yourself Saint-Denis's man on this river and that the toll men will know what it means. On the Scheldt it will mean something else.

Thirteen hundred pennies and four pegs in the abbot's field, where the booths stand at the fair in the month of the vintage. He wants three casks of Rhine wine from you before the next one, and will pay well over the price. The cart goes off at a walk. Nobody on the landing kneels, since nobody has been told.

The cellarer counts out six hundred and waits for you to ask for the rest. When you do not, he looks at you for the first time. He says he will have your name read with the benefactors, and that he has known the house pay two thousand for less. The men pull easier going down the river than they did coming up.
Two saints

The abbot's answer has come from the palace, and with it news from the west: the house of Saint Medard at Soissons is showing the people the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. The steward does not know what to think. You do.
They cannot lie in two places. The abbot writes that he took them back from Soissons once already, after Easter, with his own hands, and that he is too old to do it every year.
Let Soissons show what it likes. The blind see here. A girl from Furnes, a man from Alphen with two crutches. I have a sheet of names, with the days.
It is strange. The pedlars say there are healings at Soissons. Here we have had candles and crowds, and nothing I can write down.
The deacon says the linen was sewn with sail twine when it came. I told him boats are wet places and things get mended in them.
Whatever Soissons has, you brought us what you were given, under the seal. The abbot says pay the Frisian in good silver. So.
This year the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter came to Saint Bavo at Ganda, and the same year the house of Saint Medard said that it had them. Each house wrote down its own miracles.
This year two houses said that they had the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. The healings were at Soissons.
Take the steward's silver, and keep the finger bone you held back
Tell the steward everything, and lay the Soissons silver on the altar (900 d)

Six hundred pennies from the steward, on top of nine hundred from a bag in the dark. And in a twist of red silk in your sea chest, one small bone that came out of the bundle marked P and never went back. Two abbeys have a saint each. You have a secret, and a finger of Peter who drove out devils, and you will have to decide for yourself what the two are worth together.

The steward sits down. When you have finished he is quiet for a time, and then he sends the canon out. The nine hundred goes on the altar in its own bag. He pays you the six hundred anyway, because the abbot's letter says to, and he says that a man who will tell this at Ganda can tell it at the palace if he is asked, and that the abbey looks after its witnesses. What the abbot does about the boxes is the abbot's affair.
The book

A monk is copying a new book in the porch for the light: the abbot Einhard's own account of how the martyrs came out of Rome and what they did afterwards. He reads a little of it aloud to anyone who stands still.
Four books of it. The notary at the tomb by night, the priest of Soissons with his hand in the box, the blood, the dreams, the blind, the lame. He leaves out nothing that happened on land.
The boat to Ganda? They came there, he says, and the day. No shipman's name. A notary has a name. A blind man has a name. Boats arrive.
Of the box that went to Soissons he writes with great anger and very little ink. He names a wind, and Frisians in general.
He has heard that Soissons shows the same martyrs. He writes that God knows where his saints lie, and that he, Einhard, also knows.
And the archchaplain is archchaplain no longer. He stood with the emperor's sons in the year of the troubles and lost his abbeys for it. They say he will have some of them back. Great men float.
The abbot himself was here in the spring, sick, and could not ride. He had the sheets of the cures brought to his bed and corrected the Latin.
Ask him to read the part about the river again
Pay him to copy the leaf with the blind man of the coast on it (20 d)
Send three hundred pennies to Ganda for a lamp before the martyrs, wherever they lie

He reads it again, slowly, a finger under each word, and puts it into your tongue after. You begin to hear where one word stops and the next begins. When he tires of it he asks you a riddle about a chest that is full of wisdom and has none itself, and goes back to his ruling.

One leaf, ruled and written in an afternoon: Germar, blind, from the coast of the Frisians by the mouth of the Scheldt, and the day he saw. The monk points to the place where it says they came. That, he says, is you. It is the word for arriving.

The monk writes it down as given by a shipman for the lamp of the martyrs, and asks which house you mean. You say Ganda. He says oil burns the same before any box, and that the martyrs at least will know where to look for it.
The bones of two martyrs of Rome have come by boat to Saint Bavo's at Ganda. They say the blind see there.
The martyrs that the abbot of Ganda sent to his own house have turned up at Soissons. They say a Frisian boat lost her way in the Scheldt, and found it again in the Seine.
A river landing under a Roman wall on a spring morning; a thin young deacon holds a long box sewn in waxed linen against his chest and talks up to a Frisian in a small boat; grain sacks behind him.
The same boat at a busy landing, grey noon; a well-fed priest in a good dark cloak sits on the gunwale holding out a small purse; far up the bank the deacon walks away with his back turned.

The boat under sail at dusk on a wide river; the deacon stands at the stern singing over the stern board; a sick boy reaches two fingers toward the linen; the steersman watches the box, not the river.
A cloth spread on a muddy landing in flat afternoon light; small bones, a tooth and a knot of hair, each with a parchment strip; a lean southern man with a mule holds up two bundles of red silk.
A beach of drawn-up boats under dunes, a windy bright day; a blind man in a short Frisian cloak, led by a small child, turns his face up to a boat's stern; boatmen look away.
The boat afloat at the edge of a wide strand, the tide running out past her; on the sand a priest stands beside a horse and a servant; up the path, small, a church with its door shut; evening light.

Night in the bottom of the boat under a slack sail; four bundles of red silk side by side on the boards, two with parchment labels; a merchant's hands above them; the priest's shape against the stars, a bag at his feet.
The small boat hard pressed among sandbanks under a lead sky; white water on the shoals; three men looking back at the stern board instead of ahead.
A riverbank landing on the Channel coast, cold morning; a toll man with a tally stick looks at the water; beside him a young clerk reads from an unfolded letter and points at the boat's stern.

Where two rivers meet, bright July noon; canons in white stand along the bank with lit candles; boys run in the shallows; the small boat comes in with the long box at her stern and a blind man in her bows.

ENDING, Saint Bavo: inside a low stone church at Ganda; the box under a cloth before the altar among many candles, two crutches leaning by the door; the steward reads a short letter to a Frisian while a canon writes a list.

ENDING, Soissons: the landing of Saint-Denis in autumn light; an ox cart with a white cloth turned back from the sealed box; a cellarer counts pennies in tens on the cart's tail; the priest of Soissons smiles; nobody kneels.

ENDING, two saints: the steward's room at Ganda; he holds one letter in each hand and looks from one to the other; the Frisian stands before him with a closed face and one hand shut on something small.
A church porch in clear morning light; a monk at a sloped desk copies from one book into another, a finger on the line; a merchant stands listening with his cap in his hand; the river beyond.
